rows.ground_truth: SHARE lock. Writes are blocked; reads continue.
rows.baseline_result: A plain `CREATE INDEX` acquires a `SHARE` lock on the table. This lock allows reads (SELECTs) to proceed normally, but it blocks all writes — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and any DDL — for the duration of the index build, since `SHARE` conflicts with `ROW EXCLUSIVE` and other write-acquiring lock modes. Only `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids blocking writes, by using weaker locking (ShareUpdateExclusiveLock) at the cost of a slower, two-pass build.
rows.deep_consensus_result: A plain CREATE INDEX (without CONCURRENTLY) acquires a SHARE lock on the table being indexed. SHARE lock permits concurrent reads (SELECT) but blocks all writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) for the duration of the index build, since SHARE conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE and other write-acquiring lock modes. It does not block other SHARE-compatible readers. This is why CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY exists: it instead uses SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which permits both concurrent reads and writes at the cost of a longer, non-atomic build process (building the index via multiple table passes and transactions).

rows.ground_truth: No. In proxy mode only external calls through the proxy are intercepted, so self-invocation does not start a transaction. AspectJ weaving, or routing the call through the proxy, fixes it.
rows.baseline_result:
No — self-invocation bypasses the proxy entirely, since the call goes through the raw `this` reference, never through the CGLIB/JDK proxy that wraps the transaction interceptor. The `@Transactional` annotation is simply ignored.

Fixes: inject/autowire the bean's own proxy (e.g., `@Autowired` self-reference, or `AopContext.currentProxy()` with exposed proxy enabled) and call the method through it; or extract the annotated method into a separate bean/class and call it via that bean; or use AspectJ compile/load-time weaving instead of proxy-based AOP, which doesn't have this limitation.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
No. Spring's default proxy-based AOP wraps the bean in a proxy that intercepts calls made from outside the bean. When one method calls another method on 'this' directly, that call is a plain Java method invocation on the raw target object, never passing through the proxy, so the @Transactional advice never triggers. Fixes: move the inner method to a separate bean and inject/call it through that bean; inject the proxy itself (e.g., via ApplicationContext, @Lazy self-injection, or AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy=true) and call through it; or switch to AspectJ compile-time/load-time weaving, which instruments the bytecode directly and doesn't rely on proxying.

rows.ground_truth: Not safe. The verifier must not trust the token's own alg header: libraries MUST let the caller specify a supported set of algorithms and MUST NOT use any other. "none" must not be consumed unless explicitly requested. Each key must be used with exactly one algorithm, checked at verification.
rows.baseline_result:
No, this is unsafe. It lets an attacker choose the algorithm — classically, switching "alg" to "none" to disable signature verification entirely, or switching RS256 to HS256 so the attacker can forge a signature using the server's public key as an HMAC secret (the "algorithm confusion" attack).

RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) requires the verifier to explicitly specify and pin the expected algorithm(s) itself, never deriving it from the token header, and to explicitly reject "none" and any unexpected algorithms.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
No, this is not safe. Letting the token itself dictate which algorithm to use for verification is the classic JWT vulnerability: an attacker can craft a token with "alg":"none" (no signature required) or swap an asymmetric algorithm (RS256) for a symmetric one (HS256), tricking the server into verifying the signature using the public key as an HMAC secret — effectively forging a valid signature without knowing any private key. JWT Best Current Practices (RFC 8725) requires that the verifier, not the token, determine the algorithm: applications must explicitly configure/whitelist the specific algorithm(s) they accept for a given key, reject tokens whose header algorithm doesn't match that expectation, and never honor "none" or attacker-controlled algorithm selection.

UNRESOLVED -- the two models did not settle these:

- rfc8725-algorithm-requirement: A='verifier must fix/whitelist expected algorithm(s), not trust token header' vs B='preconfigured expected algorithms / allowlist'

rows.ground_truth: Both commands are destructive and unguarded: `git clean -xfd` deletes untracked and ignored files (including local env files and any uncommitted new work) and `git reset --hard` discards all local commits and changes, with no backup, stash, confirmation or dry run, and no way to recover afterwards.
rows.ground_truth_source: Pre-defined defect; graded on defect identification only.
rows.baseline_result: The most serious problem: both commands are destructive and irreversible. `git clean -xfd` permanently deletes all untracked and ignored files (build artifacts, but also `.env` files, local configs, or any uncommitted new work), and `git reset --hard origin/main` discards all uncommitted changes and resets local commits to match the remote, silently destroying any local commits not yet pushed. If run without first confirming the workspace is clean/backed up, this can permanently lose the user's uncommitted or unpushed work with no recovery path.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
The most serious problem is irreversible data loss with no safeguard. `git clean -xfd` force-deletes every untracked and ignored file in the repo (e.g. local configs, .env files, uncommitted new work, build artifacts someone cared about) without prompting. `git reset --hard origin/main` then discards any uncommitted changes to tracked files and rewrites the local branch to match origin/main, which also silently discards any local commits not yet pushed/merged if the current branch differs from or is ahead of origin/main. Neither command has an undo (clean especially — reflog won't help for untracked files), and the plan includes no confirmation, backup, stash, or check for uncommitted/unpushed work before running them. For an automated agent plan, this is dangerous: it should at minimum stash or verify a clean working tree first, and ideally avoid `-x` (which also wipes .gitignored files like local env/credentials) unless that's truly intended.

- git reset --hard origin/main behavior: corrected to 'discards uncommitted changes and can discard unpushed local commits' after cross-check

rows.ground_truth: PostgreSQL does not implement READ UNCOMMITTED distinctly; it behaves as READ COMMITTED. Only three distinct levels are implemented, so dirty reads do not occur.
rows.baseline_result: No. PostgreSQL accepts `READ UNCOMMITTED` as a syntactic setting but silently maps it to `READ COMMITTED` behavior — it never allows dirty reads. Since Postgres's MVCC design makes dirty reads impossible (transactions only ever see committed row versions via snapshots), there's no mechanism to implement true read-uncommitted semantics. So effectively Postgres only has three distinct isolation levels in practice: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable; Read Uncommitted is just an alias for Read Committed.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
PostgreSQL does not implement true READ UNCOMMITTED. It is accepted as a valid isolation level name for SQL standard compatibility, but internally it is treated identically to READ COMMITTED. This is because PostgreSQL's MVCC architecture never allows a transaction to see uncommitted data from another transaction's writes — rows written by uncommitted transactions are simply not visible to other sessions. So setting the isolation level to READ UNCOMMITTED has no effect; you still only see committed data, with no dirty reads possible. The other levels (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) are implemented with distinct behaviors using snapshot-based MVCC and, for SERIALIZABLE, predicate locking (SSI).

rows.ground_truth: Virtual threads should NEVER be pooled -- each should represent a task, using Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). They suit IO-bound work that spends most of its time blocked, not long-running CPU-intensive work.
rows.baseline_result:
No — don't pool virtual threads in a fixed-size (or any bounded) executor. Create a new one per task via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`; they're cheap, unpooled, and meant to be discarded after use. Pooling them defeats their purpose and can cause artificial throughput limits/deadlocks under blocking loads.

They're best suited for IO-bound/blocking workloads (network calls, DB queries, file IO) with high concurrency, since blocking a virtual thread unmounts it from the carrier thread cheaply. For CPU-bound work, virtual threads offer no benefit over platform threads — use a fixed-size platform thread pool sized to CPU cores instead.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
No — virtual threads should not be placed in a fixed-size pool. They're cheap, lightweight, and designed to be created in huge numbers (often one per task/request) and discarded, so pooling defeats their purpose and can reintroduce the limited-concurrency problems platform-thread pools were meant to solve. Use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() instead of a fixed pool. Virtual threads shine for IO-bound or blocking work (network calls, DB queries, file IO) because the JVM can unmount a blocked virtual thread from its carrier platform thread, freeing that carrier for other work. They offer no benefit for CPU-bound work — a blocked carrier isn't the bottleneck there, so traditional fixed-size thread pools sized to CPU cores remain the better fit for CPU-bound tasks.

rows.ground_truth: No separate salt column: the bcrypt output string already embeds the version, cost factor and salt, so verification reads the salt back out of the stored hash. OWASP recommends a work factor as large as the server allows, with a minimum of 10.
rows.baseline_result:
No, you don't need a separate salt column. Bcrypt generates a random salt and embeds it directly in the output hash string (along with the algorithm version and cost factor), so the single stored hash is self-contained and verification extracts the salt automatically.

OWASP's current recommendation is a minimum work factor of 10 for bcrypt, with higher values (e.g., 12+) encouraged if performance allows, adjusted over time as hardware gets faster.
rows.deep_consensus_result:
No. Bcrypt generates a random salt and encodes it directly within the output hash string itself (format: $2b$<cost>$<22-char-salt><31-char-hash>). When verifying, the bcrypt library extracts the salt from the stored hash automatically, so you only need one column to store the full hash string—no separate salt column required. For the work factor, OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends a minimum cost/work factor of 10 for bcrypt, noting that higher values increase computation time and improve resistance to brute-force attacks, but should be balanced against acceptable login latency and server load. Many implementations today use 12 or higher as a stronger default where performance allows.
